resources.title: Big-O Cheat Sheet
resources.description: Complexity classes, what fits in a one-second limit, and C++ container costs.
resources.body:
# Big-O Cheat Sheet

## Common orders, fastest to slowest

| Order | Name | Typical source |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | hash lookup, array index |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | binary search, balanced tree descent |
| O(n) | linear | single pass over the input |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | comparison sorts, divide and conquer |
| O(n²) | quadratic | nested loop over the same input |
| O(2ⁿ) | exponential | subset enumeration, naive recursion |
| O(n!) | factorial | permutation enumeration |

## What fits in one second

A rough budget for a 1-second limit, assuming simple operations:

| n up to | Order you need |
|---|---|
| 10 | O(n!) or O(2ⁿ) |
| 20 | O(2ⁿ) |
| 500 | O(n³) |
| 5,000 | O(n²) |
| 10⁶ | O(n log n) |
| 10⁸ | O(n) |

Use this to work *backwards*: the constraint tells you the complexity you are
aiming for before you write a line of code. If n ≤ 20, an exponential search is
probably intended. If n = 10⁵, anything quadratic will time out.

## C++ container operations

| Container | Access | Insert | Search |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vector` | O(1) | O(1) amortised at the back | O(n) |
| `deque` | O(1) | O(1) at either end | O(n) |
| `set` / `map` | — | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| `unordered_set` / `unordered_map` | — | O(1) average | O(1) average, O(n) worst |
| `priority_queue` | O(1) top | O(log n) | — |

`unordered_*` is average-case O(1) but degrades to O(n) on collisions. In a
contest with adversarial tests, an ordered `map` with a guaranteed O(log n) is
sometimes the safer choice.

## Space counts too

Recursion costs stack space proportional to its depth. A recursive DFS over 10⁶
nodes will overflow the stack long before it runs out of time.

resources.title: C++ STL Quick Reference
resources.description: The containers, algorithms, and idioms you reach for most in a contest.
resources.body:
# C++ STL Quick Reference

Everything here needs `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` or the specific header.

## Sequence containers

```cpp
vector<int> v = {3, 1, 2};
v.push_back(4);          // append
v.pop_back();            // remove last
v.size(); v.empty();
sort(v.begin(), v.end());              // ascending
sort(v.rbegin(), v.rend());            // descending
reverse(v.begin(), v.end());
```

## Sorting with a custom comparator

```cpp
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
    return a.second < b.second;   // true means "a comes first"
});
```

The comparator must be a *strict weak ordering* — return `false` for equal
elements, never `<=`, or you get undefined behaviour.

## Binary search (on a sorted range)

```cpp
bool found     = binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), x);
auto first_ge  = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x);  // first element >= x
auto first_gt  = upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x);  // first element  > x
int  index     = first_ge - v.begin();
int  count_of_x = upper_bound(...) - lower_bound(...);
```

## Associative containers

```cpp
map<string,int> m;            // sorted by key, O(log n)
m["a"]++;                     // default-constructs to 0 first
if (m.count("a")) { ... }
for (auto& [key, value] : m) { ... }   // C++17 structured binding

unordered_map<string,int> um; // hash table, O(1) average
set<int> s; s.insert(5);      // sorted, unique
multiset<int> ms;             // sorted, duplicates allowed
```

## Heaps

```cpp
priority_queue<int> maxHeap;                                   // largest on top
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minHeap;        // smallest on top
maxHeap.push(3); maxHeap.top(); maxHeap.pop();
```

## Strings

```cpp
string s = "hello";
s.substr(1, 3);              // "ell" — (start, length), not (start, end)
s.find("ll");                // index, or string::npos
to_string(42); stoi("42"); stoll("42");
transform(s.begin(), s.end(), s.begin(), ::tolower);
```

## Fast input

Large inputs time out on `cin` unless you unsync it:

```cpp
ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
cin.tie(nullptr);
```

Do not mix `cin` and `scanf` after doing this.

## Useful numeric helpers

```cpp
__gcd(a, b);                        // GCD
max({a, b, c}); min({a, b, c});     // more than two arguments
accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);  // note the 0LL — 0 overflows on big sums
count(v.begin(), v.end(), x);
```

Watch the accumulator type: `accumulate(..., 0)` sums into an `int` and
overflows silently even when the vector holds `long long`.

resources.title: SQL Joins Cheat Sheet
resources.description: INNER vs LEFT, the WHERE-clause trap that silently undoes an outer join, and counting correctly.
resources.body:
# SQL Joins Cheat Sheet

Given two tables:

```
users            orders
-----            ------
id  name         id  user_id  total
1   Ana          1   1        50
2   Ben          2   1        30
3   Cara         3   2        20
```

## INNER JOIN — rows matching on both sides

```sql
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

Ana/50, Ana/30, Ben/20. **Cara disappears** — she has no orders.

## LEFT JOIN — every left row, matched or not

```sql
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

Ana/50, Ana/30, Ben/20, **Cara/NULL**. This is the one you want for "list every
user and their order count, including users with none".

## The classic LEFT JOIN mistake

```sql
-- WRONG: the WHERE turns this back into an INNER JOIN
SELECT u.name FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.total > 25;

-- RIGHT: filter inside the join condition
SELECT u.name FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.total > 25;
```

Any `WHERE` condition on a right-side column discards the NULL rows the LEFT
JOIN just produced, silently undoing it.

## RIGHT JOIN / FULL OUTER JOIN

`RIGHT JOIN` is `LEFT JOIN` with the tables swapped — most people just swap
them and keep using LEFT. `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both
sides.

## Counting with joins

```sql
-- WRONG: COUNT(*) counts the NULL row too, so Cara gets 1
SELECT u.name, COUNT(*) FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.name;

-- RIGHT: COUNT(column) skips NULLs, so Cara gets 0
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.name;
```

`COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(expr)` counts non-NULL values. On an outer
join that difference is the whole answer.

## Join vs. subquery

```sql
-- "users who ordered" — a semi-join; EXISTS won't duplicate rows
SELECT name FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
```

An `INNER JOIN` returns one row *per match*, so a user with three orders
appears three times. Use `EXISTS` (or `DISTINCT`) when you only want to know
whether a match exists.
